sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: With the emergence and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, the effectiveness of traditional antibiotics has gradually declined, posing a major global public health challenge. The World Health Organization (WHO) lists drug-resistant infections among the top global public health threats [1]. Antibacterial peptides (ABPs) are small peptides with natural antibacterial activity [2]. They kill bacteria mainly by disrupting the cell membrane, a mechanism that reduces the likelihood of resistance [3]. ABPs exhibit high efficacy [4] and relatively low toxicity [5], making them attractive for research [6]. In recent years, progress in ABP research has been substantial. A large number of peptides with antibacterial activity have been identified from diverse organisms, and their structures and functions have been studied in depth [7]. Although traditional wet-lab methods remain important for evaluating ABP activity, they are costly and time-consuming [8]. Artificial intelligence techniques can predict ABP activity without relying on specific experimental conditions, providing an efficient pre-screening step before wet-lab evaluation.

Although these methods have shown progress in predicting ABP MIC values, their overall predictive accuracy remains insufficient for reliable practical use. Most methods rely on single-modality or single-scale feature representations, and fail to integrate multi-level information, such as the ABP sequence and its corresponding 3D structure, making it difficult to capture the complex relationships among sequence, structure, function, and antibacterial mechanisms. As a result, important interactions between structural features and function may be overlooked. Moreover, many studies train and evaluate models on datasets that are small in size or limited in species diversity. This lack of diverse data hampers cross-species generalization and reduces model robustness in real-world applications, thereby constraining its potential for clinical translation.

To address these challenges, we propose the geometric graph network (GGN)-ABPMIC model, integrating multi-modal peptide sequence features and multi-scale structural features. The features are processed through a GGN, and the resulting outputs are concatenated with peptide descriptors and fed into a regression head to predict MIC values. In addition, we introduce a novel multi-stage dynamic-weight hybrid loss function (MDH-loss), which combines mean squared error (MSE), the Huber loss [16], and a contrastive learning loss [17] to enhance training stability. We evaluate the model on datasets from 10 bacterial species, and GGN-ABPMIC achieves strong predictive performance across all datasets, demonstrating notable cross-species generalization.

sec.title: Dataset

caption.p: Summary of ABP datasets for different bacterial species.

sec.p: We randomly split the datasets into training and test sets at an 8:2 ratio. To validate the effectiveness of this split, we compared the amino acid composition between the training and test datasets across all 10 datasets. As shown in Supplementary Figs S2 and S3, the amino acid frequency distributions are highly concordant between the training and test datasets, with no detectable compositional bias introduced by the split.This supports the expectation that feature learning will generalize beyond the training dataset.

We similarly evaluated the consistency of sequence length distributions between the training and test datasets. Supplementary Figs S4 and S5 reveal highly similar distribution patterns and central tendencies for both sets, indicating that the split maintains strong representativeness at the structural level. Collectively, these results affirm that the data partition provides a reliable and balanced foundation for subsequent model training and evaluation.

sec.title: Model architecture
sec.p: To comprehensively characterize ABP activity, we designed a computational framework that integrates sequence-derived and structure-derived information, as illustrated in Fig. 1A. The pipeline starts with ABP sequences, from which ESMFold [27] predicts their 3D structure. We then extract multi-scale features from both the sequences and the predicted structures in parallel and integrate them with ProtTrans [28] embeddings and the definition of secondary structure of proteins (DSSP) [29], which provides residue-level secondary structure annotations and structure-derived descriptors. All features are then fed into the GGN framework for processing, and the resulting representation is concatenated with conventional peptide descriptors. The combined features are fed into a regression module to predict the activity value. During training, we apply MDH-loss with weights dynamically updated across epochs to balance the optimization of the regression head and the GGN encoder. The loss is backpropagated end-to-end, enabling the joint learning of all components.

caption.p: Architecture of the GGN-ABPMIC model. (A) Overall workflow of the model. (B) Detailed workflow of the GGN. (C) Core mechanism of the GVP. DSSP, define secondary structure of protein; AAC, amino acid composition; DPC, dipeptide composition; PCP, physicochemical properties.

graphic.alt-text: Schematic diagram showing the overall GGN-ABPMIC prediction pipeline, the internal structure of the geometric graph network, and the update mechanism of the geometric vector perceptron for antimicrobial peptide activity prediction

sec.p: Figure 1B provides a detailed illustration of the workflow of the GGN. Node features and edge features are fed in parallel into different geometric vector perceptrons (GVPs), followed by message aggregation through the message-passing layers, thereby fully capturing domain-specific information. The graph representations obtained after the message-passing layers are subsequently processed by a specialized GVP that normalizes all features into scalar form, and the output features are finally obtained through a pooling layer.

Within a GVP layer, scalar and vector features are updated through tightly coupled operations. As shown in Fig. 1C, the vector features undergo a linear projection, and the L2 norms of these projected vectors are computed to capture rotation-invariant geometric information. This norm is concatenated with the input scalar features and passed through nonlinear fully connected layers to produce updated scalar features. In parallel, the projected vector features are processed by a separate linear transformation to yield candidate vector features, which are then gated and scaled using the scalar outputs to produce updated vector features. This resulting tuples preserve geometric sensitivity while remaining rotation-invariant.

sec.title: Edge features
G‌GN
GNN
sec.p: GNNs [30] have achieved significant progress in protein structure learning, especially in capturing residue–residue interactions and topological relationships. However, conventional GNNs face fundamental limitations in handling 3D geometric features. Typically, a protein is represented as a proximity graph, and geometric information (such as atomic coordinates and spatial orientation) is encoded into rotation-invariant scalar features, often by constructing local coordinate systems to compute relative distances or angles. While this simplification preserves rotational invariance, it discards critical geometric information: Vector features carrying spatial relationships are reduced to scalars, preventing the model from perceiving directionality and shape variations in 3D space. In addition, reliance on local coordinate frames increases computational complexity and hampers learning of global geometric patterns, limiting the expressiveness for tasks such as structure prediction and design. To address these challenges, we introduce GGN [31]. Its primary advantage is the use of GVPs to directly process vector features while jointly updating scalar and vector channels. This design preserves geometric sensitivity and rotational invariance simultaneously, effectively overcoming the limitations of traditional GNNs in handling 3D geometric information. The workflow of GGN is detailed in the following sections.

sec.title: GVP
sec.p: GVP [32] is an innovative neural network module with unique advantages for handling multi-modal geometric features in biomolecular structures. By simultaneously processing scalar and vector features, it overcomes the limitations of conventional graph neural networks in geometric reasoning. The core strength of GVP lies in its ability to directly operate on Euclidean vectors while maintaining equivariance or invariance under rotations and reflections, enabling efficient modeling of protein structures. This module can serve as a replacement for standard fully connected layers, and when integrated into GNNs, it enhances the network’s sensitivity to geometric relationships. In ABP activity prediction, GVP effectively captures the synergistic information from both sequence and structural features.

Two separate GVPs are used to compute and propagate node and edge features. The features produced by GVP are used to construct the input graph representation, which is then fed into the GVP-based GNN.

sec.title: Message passing layer
sec.p: The message passing layer is the core component of GGN, designed to update node features through iterative information exchange, thereby integrating relational reasoning with geometric reasoning. The workflow of this layer involves three key steps: first, generating message vectors to encode local structural information; second, aggregating messages and updating node states; and third, applying a pointwise feedforward layer for deeper feature transformation. This process ensures equivariance of geometric features and stability of scalar features, providing a foundation for protein structure modeling.

In the message generation step, message vectors are formed by combining source node features and edge features, followed by processing through a GVP. These vectors are then passed to the target node, capturing local geometric relationships between nodes.

After message generation, the target node aggregates all incoming messages and updates its state using residual connections, dropout, and layer normalization. Node aggregation integrates neighborhood information while maintaining training stability.

Following message passing, a pointwise feedforward layer is applied independently to each node for deeper feature transformation, further enhancing representational capacity. Scalar and vector features are then processed through an additional GVP, and the output features are pooled using a hybrid pooling layer composed of global average pooling [33] and attention pooling [34]. Average pooling ensures model robustness and prevents prediction instability, while attention pooling enhances discriminative power by amplifying important signals and suppressing noise, thereby improving overall model performance in parallel.

sec.title: Peptide feature descriptors
sec.p: The features processed by the GGN comprehensively represent the sequence and structural information of ABPs; however, they lack numerical features such as amino acid composition and physicochemical properties, which are often related to the activity of antimicrobial peptides. Peptide feature descriptors are a set of numerical features directly extracted from ABP sequences, capturing multidimensional information, including amino acid composition, order, and physicochemical properties. When combined with structural features processed by the GGN and other sequence features, peptide feature descriptors provide complementary information, enabling a comprehensive representation of antimicrobial peptides. Based on this principle, the model includes five representative types of descriptors, each digitally encoding the peptide sequence from different perspectives.
These descriptors quantify the occurrence frequency of the 20 natural amino acids in the peptide sequence [35], reflecting basic compositional characteristics. The calculation is as follows:

Finally, these five types of peptide descriptors are concatenated to form a 553-dimensional feature vector for each sample. By integrating sequence information at different scales, this representation preserves local chemical environment features, captures long-range interaction patterns, and incorporates key physicochemical parameters, providing a comprehensive, multi-scale feature foundation for subsequent antimicrobial peptide activity prediction.

sec.title: MDH-loss
sec.p: In the regression task of predicting the MIC values of antimicrobial peptides, the complex data distribution and limited sample size make a single loss function insufficient to ensure both robustness and generalization. To address this, we design a multi-stage mixed loss function that dynamically adjusts the weights of different loss components during training. The loss function consists of three main parts: MSE, Huber loss, and a contrastive loss (ContrastLoss). During training, the weights of these components change according to the ratio of the current epoch to the total number of epochs.

sec.title: Evaluation metrics
Comparison of loss functions
sec.p: To evaluate the effect of different loss functions on ABP activity prediction, we compared the convergence curves of multiple candidate loss functions on the B. subtilis dataset to examine their optimization behavior during training. As shown in Fig. 3, Huber loss exhibits faster convergence and stronger stability in the early stage of training, indicating its advantage in rapid optimization. However, the objectives of model training vary across different stages. Early training mainly requires stable and efficient convergence, whereas the middle and later stages place greater emphasis on refining error patterns and improving final predictive performance. Therefore, the suitability of a loss function should not be judged solely by convergence speed. Although MDH-loss does not show a clear advantage in early optimization, its convergence pattern suggests that it remains effective during the subsequent training process. This indicates that the optimization behavior of different loss functions should be interpreted from a stage-dependent perspective, and a more comprehensive evaluation still requires comparison of their final predictive performance on the target task.

sec.title: Hyperparameter optimization
sec.p: In this study, when feeding the multi-scale features of ABPs into the GGN for activity regression, overfitting becomes a prominent issue. This mainly arises from the model’s complex architecture, which contains millions of parameters, while the available experimental data are limited—each dataset contains only a few hundred to a few thousand peptide sequences. To address this problem, we adopt a random dropout strategy. By randomly deactivating a subset of neurons during training, we reduce co-adaptation among neurons and enhance model robustness. Under this setting, the choice of the dropout rate becomes particularly important. Additionally, the learning rate controls the step size in gradient descent, thereby affecting optimization speed and stability. We tune it to balance training efficiency and convergence accuracy due to the anisotropic and uneven curvature of the loss landscape. Temperature controls the separation between positive and negative sample pairs in the feature space, affecting feature distribution sharpness. A proper temperature enhances the discriminability and stability of the feature space. The margin defines the minimum separation between positive and negative sample pairs in metric learning, which directly influencing decision boundaries. A suitable margin helps the model learn features with large inter-class separation and small intra-class variation.

Based on these considerations, we design a systematic grid search strategy to determine the optimal hyperparameter settings for each dataset. The specific search strategy is shown in Supplementary Table S1. For each of the 10 datasets, we conduct five repeated experiments and retain the best-performing hyperparameter combination. The final chosen hyperparameters for all datasets are reported in Table 3.

caption.p: Optimal parameters determined by grid search for each dataset.

sec.p: After the grid search optimization, the model achieved substantial improvements in key performance metrics across all 10 bacterial datasets. It captured the intrinsic patterns of ABP activity more effectively, thereby significantly enhancing prediction accuracy and reliability. More importantly, the optimized hyperparameters fundamentally improved the model’s generalization ability and robustness across different datasets.

sec.title: Model comparison
sec.p: We conducted a systematic evaluation of our model’s performance on ABP activity prediction across 10 bacterial species. As shown in Table 4, our model achieved lower MSE values on 9 out of the 10 species, with an average MSE of 0.221. This represents a 20.2% reduction compared with the baseline value of 0.277. Notably, the model obtained substantial improvements on datasets such as Acinetobacter baumannii and B. subtilis. The largest reduction was observed on the A. baumannii dataset, where MSE decreased by 54.5%, demonstrating that our model significantly enhances prediction accuracy across diverse bacterial species.

caption.p: MSE performance of the baseline model AMPActiPred and our GGN-ABPMIC model on 10 different bacterial species, along with their average values.

table-wrap-foot.p: The better values are highligthed in bold.

sec.p: On the S. aureus dataset, GGN-ABPMIC performed slightly worse than the baseline model. Given that this dataset contains a relatively large number of samples and shows no obvious difference in its overall value distribution compared with the other species, this performance gap is unlikely to be explained solely by limited data size or a simple distribution shift. A more plausible explanation is that the antibacterial activity against S. aureus is influenced by more complex biological factors, such as strain-level variation, cell wall-related mechanisms of action, and variability introduced by experimental measurement conditions. These factors may increase the effective complexity of the task and introduce additional noise. In addition, the current model mainly relies on sequence, physicochemical, and local structural descriptors, and does not explicitly encode higher-level information that may be more closely related to species-specific mechanisms of action. As a result, some discriminative patterns in the S. aureus dataset may not yet be fully captured. In future work, we plan to incorporate more mechanism-relevant features and combine them with more refined data cleaning and stratified modeling strategies to further improve prediction accuracy and robustness on this dataset.

sec.title: Visualization of prediction results
sec.p: To provide an intuitive view of predictive performance, Fig. 5 illustrates the relationship between actual activity values and predictions generated by GGN-ABPMIC on the test set. Visual inspection reveals pronounced linear alignment across all bacterial species. Data points cluster densely around the diagonal identity line. This tight conformity indicates minimal prediction error and robust fidelity.

caption.p: Visualization of the actual and predicted pMIC values across the 10 datasets.

graphic.alt-text: Scatter plots comparing actual and predicted pMIC values for 10 bacterial datasets, with point distributions indicating the agreement between experimental and predicted values

sec.p: The scatter patterns demonstrate consistent performance throughout the entire activity range. Predictions remain accurate for peptides with low to high potency. The predictions exhibit no systematic directional bias. Most species exhibit highly compact point clouds. However, subtle differences in scatter breadth are discernible among bacterial types. Predictions for A. baumannii and Micrococcus luteus show exceptionally tight clustering. This indicates superior capture of structure–activity relationships for these organisms. In contrast, S. aureus displays slightly more dispersed points. This suggests greater inherent variability for this species.

Points distribute uniformly above and below the unity line across all activity levels. This uniform distribution confirms the unbiased nature of the predictions. Collectively, these visual characteristics affirm the strong predictive capability of GGN-ABPMIC. The framework demonstrates suitability as a reliable tool for antimicrobial peptide activity prediction.

sec.title: Ablation study
sec.p: Since our study incorporates multi-scale features, including sequence-derived, physicochemical, structural, and geometry-related representations, we designed a systematic ablation study to evaluate the contribution of each component to the performance of the GGN-ABPMIC model. Five ablation settings were constructed:

list-item.p: (i) GGN-ABPMIC w/o ProtTrans: removing the ProtTrans feature embeddings.
(ii) GGN-ABPMIC w/o PFD: removing the concatenated peptide feature descriptors.
(iii) GGN-ABPMIC w/o DSSP: removing secondary structure.

(iv) GGN-ABPMIC w/o GVP: removing the original GVP-based geometric graph encoder. In this setting, geometric features that could be compressed into scalar descriptors were retained in scalar form, whereas directional vector features that could not be scalarized were removed. The resulting features were then directly processed by a standard scalar GNN.
(v) GGN-ABPMIC w/o geometric features: removing the original GVP-based geometric graph encoder together with all multi-scale geometric features.

sec.title: Case study

caption.p: Case study of several ABP sequences targeting E. coli.

sec.p: A similar pattern is observed for the remaining closely related sequences, where one or two residue substitutions lead to noticeable changes in antimicrobial activity, highlighting the sensitivity of ABP activity to the local sequence context. GGN-ABPMIC consistently produces predictions closer to the experimental values, indicating that it can better capture fine-grained structural and physicochemical differences. By contrast, AMPActiPred shows larger errors for some peptides, and no MIC estimates were generated for several others. This is related to its three-stage framework, in which the model first determines whether a peptide is an ABP, then predicts its target species, and finally estimates the MIC value for the predicted target bacterium. Therefore, the MIC prediction for E. coli requires the peptide to be identified as both an ABP and an E. coli-targeting ABP in the earlier stages. Although the fifth sequence is highly homologous to the fourth and sixth sequences, subtle sequence variations may have prevented its correct classification. Overall, these results further support the practical utility of GGN-ABPMIC in ABP discovery.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, we proposed GGN-ABPMIC, a GGN-based model for predicting the MIC values of ABPs. A systematic evaluation across datasets from 10 bacterial species showed that GGN-ABPMIC achieves excellent predictive performance and strong generalization ability in ABP activity prediction.

The GGN-ABPMIC model integrates multi-scale features from different ABP modalities. These features are processed through a GGN and then combined with multiple peptide feature descriptors for MIC prediction. We also designed an MDH-loss that incorporates MSE, the Huber loss, and a contrastive learning loss to enhance the model’s robustness in regression tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that GGN-ABPMIC outperforms the existing method AMPActiPred on the vast majority of strain categories.

In addition, we validated the effectiveness of each model component through hyperparameter tuning and ablation studies. For hyperparameter tuning, we designed a systematic grid-search strategy to identify the optimal hyperparameter settings for each dataset. In the ablation experiments, we assessed the contributions of ProTrans, peptide feature descriptors, and multi-scale geometric features. The results show that these components, along with the hybrid loss function, all contribute significantly to improving prediction performance.

In summary, GGN-ABPMIC demonstrates clear advantages in predicting the MIC of ABPs, providing an efficient and accurate computational approach for ABP drug development. In future work, we plan to further expand the dataset and optimize the model architecture to improve prediction performance and broaden the model’s application scope.

list-item.p: Geometric graph network-antibacterial peptides minimum inhibitory concentration (GGN-ABPMIC) is introduced for the prediction of minimum inhibitory concentration of antimicrobial peptides based on multi-scale geometric graph networks and dynamic loss functions.

GGN-ABPMIC integrates information from geometric graph at atomic- and residue-scales. It uses scalar features and vector features. By incorporating diverse peptide feature descriptors, it overcomes the limitations of traditional methods that rely on a single sequence feature.

To address complex data distributions and overfitting, we design a multi-stage, dynamically weighted hybrid loss function. It combines mean squared error loss, Huber loss, and contrastive loss. The component weights are updated throughout training epochs.
Case analyses show that GGN-ABPMIC exhibits high predictive accuracy for unseen sequences. Compared with existing methods, its MIC predictions are closer to the true MIC values.
